text:
Alfred North Whitehead was an English mathematician and philosopher known for his foundational work in mathematical logic and process philosophy. Born in 1861, he initially excelled in mathematics, earning a B.A. from Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1884. He later collaborated with Bertrand Russell on *Principia Mathematica* (1910–13), a seminal work in mathematical logic, before transitioning to philosophy. Whitehead rejected the Cartesian view of reality as composed of static matter, proposing instead an "event-based" or "process" ontology where all entities are interrelated occasions of experience. He developed the concept of "prehension" to describe how entities incorporate aspects of their environment, and his "philosophy of organism" emphasized creativity, change, and the interconnectedness of all things.
Whitehead's influence extended significantly into theology, education, and the sciences. His ideas inspired the development of process theology, particularly through the work of Charles Hartshorne, and influenced figures like John B. Cobb and David Ray Griffin. In education, he argued against rote learning of "inert ideas," advocating for a transdisciplinary approach that integrates imagination and values. His complex philosophical writings, such as *Science and the Modern World* (1925) and *Process and Reality* (1929), challenged prevailing scientific materialism and offered a metaphysical framework that anticipated modern concerns in physics, ecology, and sustainability. Although his prose remains notoriously difficult, his thought has seen a resurgence in recent decades, especially within constructive postmodern thought and environmental ethics.
